title: The Second John: Burlington, the Laboratory School, and the Chair in Coyoacan
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Burlington, birth at 186 South Willard Street
stops.date_confidence: attested; the chronology's entry 1859.10.20 gives the day. The pin is the geocode of 186 South Willard Street, correcting a dossier coordinate that fell some 570 m southwest of the address.
stops.campa: In a house on South Willard Street, Lucina Rich and Archibald Sprague Dewey give their third son the name of their second. The first John Archibald, born three years earlier, died that January, and the family sets the name on the boy who comes in October, as families did then. Archibald keeps a grocery on the lake side of town, near the wharves. The Daily Free Press carried the elder boy's death; the deed to the house is dated August, two months before the birth.
suggested_refs: The Dewey family house at 186 South Willard Street, Burlington, purchased August 1859
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1859.01.18, 1859.08.20, 1859.10.20
Daily Free Press, Burlington, cited in the same chronology for the elder brother's death

stops.name: Cumberland, the last winter of the war
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; the chronology's 1864 entry records the move and quotes Jane Dewey's phrase, with no month. The pin marks the county seat, since no house-level site was found; a dossier coordinate placing the family 28 km south, in Charlotte and Prince Edward county territory, is not followed here.
stops.campa: Archibald has gone to the army as a quartermaster, and for one winter the family follows him south into Virginia. Cumberland is tobacco land and courthouse roads, a long way from a lakeside grocery, and the daughter Jane, writing the family's account seventy-five years afterward, calls it the last winter of the war. What a four-year-old took from a Confederate county under Union occupation nobody set down. The Deweys are back in Burlington inside three years and the boy is entered in the town's grammar school.
suggested_refs: Jane Dewey's biography of her father in The Philosophy of John Dewey (1939)
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1864, citing Dewey correspondence 1933.07.29 and Neil Coughlan, Young John Dewey

stops.name: Burlington, District School No. 3
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; chronology entry 1867.09 for the school and 1867-1876 for the George Street residence. Day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The family settles on George Street and the boy is entered in District School No. 3, later called the North Grammar School. Burlington is a lake port of lumber wharves and mills, with the university standing on the hill above the town. He passes from the grammar school into Burlington High School. Nine years run between the return from Virginia and his matriculation, and the record of them is an address and the name of a school. Whether the boy was any good at either, it does not say.
suggested_refs: The North Grammar School, Burlington, and the family residence at 14 George Street
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1867.09 and 1867-1876

stops.name: University of Vermont, the limits of political economy
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1875.09 for matriculation and 1879.06.25 for the degree and oration, the latter citing the Burlington Free Press Times of 26 June 1879.
stops.campa: He enters at fifteen and takes the degree at nineteen. Philosophy comes late in the course and comes through H. A. P. Torrey, who goes on teaching him privately for years after the diploma. At the commencement of the twenty-fifth of June he delivers the oration, Limits of Political Economy, holding that the science of wealth cannot stand as the science of man; the Burlington Free Press Times prints the day in its issue of the twenty-sixth. Phi Beta Kappa, Delta Psi. No position waits for him.
suggested_refs: The 1879 commencement programme, University of Vermont
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1875.09 and 1879.06.25
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, John Dewey

stops.name: Oil City, the assistant principal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1879 to June 1881; the chronology gives no arrival date. The month here is set to the school year following the June commencement, to hold the travel order, and is an inference, not a documented date. Roberta Lowitz's 1904 birth in this town is attested at chronology entry 1946.12.11.
stops.campa: He goes south into the Pennsylvania oil country as assistant principal of the high school at Oil City, teaching classics, the sciences, and algebra to the children of a boom town of derricks and refineries. It is his first paid work and it lasts two years. He is twenty when he arrives and has published nothing at all. In 1904, twenty-three years after he leaves this town, a girl named Roberta Lowitz is born in it. He will marry her in a New York apartment when he is eighty-seven.
suggested_refs: Oil City High School, Pennsylvania, Dewey's first appointment
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1879-1881.06, citing Alan Ryan, John Dewey, and Coughlan, Young John Dewey

stops.name: Charlotte, Lake View Seminary
stops.date_confidence: attested for the academic year 1881-1882; the chronology gives no month, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Back in Vermont he takes charge of the small Lake View Seminary at Charlotte, a farming village on the lake shore south of Burlington, and teaches there as its principal. Weekends he goes up to Torrey in Burlington and reads philosophy with him, the same private tutorial that began at the university and is kept up now by a schoolmaster paying his own way. The Gazetteer and Business Directory of Chittenden County for 1882 lists him at the school by name. He is twenty-two, and this is the last year of it.
suggested_refs: Gazetteer and Business Directory of Chittenden County, Vermont, 1882-83
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1881-1882

stops.name: Johns Hopkins, the rooms on Saratoga Street
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1882-1884; month and day defaulted to 01. The pin marks the old downtown campus.
stops.campa: He arrives in Baltimore at twenty-three as a graduate student in a philosophy department only a few years old, at a university built on the German model, where research is the point and the professor need not be a clergyman. George Sylvester Morris teaches him Hegel, G. Stanley Hall runs the psychological laboratory, Charles Sanders Peirce lectures on logic and is thought difficult. Two years of this and the schoolmaster from the lake port has a profession. He lodges at 66 Saratoga Street and afterward at 91.
suggested_refs: The Johns Hopkins Metaphysical Club, and the university's original downtown campus
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1882-1884

stops.name: Johns Hopkins, the dissertation that does not survive
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1884.06.05, citing Johns Hopkins University Circulars 3, no. 31 (June 1884): 119. That no text of the dissertation survives is stated in the chronology's own note and confirmed by the absence of any printed version.
stops.campa: On the fifth of June the university circulars record the degree. The dissertation is called The Psychology of Kant, and no copy of it survives: not in Baltimore, not in the thirty-seven volumes of the collected works, not anywhere. His first sustained piece of philosophy is the one piece of it nobody can read. He spent the next fifty years working his way out of Kant, arguing against the partition between a mind that knows and a world set over against it. Whether that argument had already started here, there is no way to find out.
suggested_refs: Johns Hopkins University Circulars 3, no. 31 (June 1884), 119
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1884.06.05

stops.name: Ann Arbor, instructor in philosophy
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1884.07.19, citing the Proceedings of the Board of Regents, June 1884, 482. The church membership and its 1898 closure are chronology entry 1884.11.02, citing the Membership Roll 1847-1906 of the First Congregational Church of Ann Arbor.
stops.campa: Morris has taken the Michigan chair and brings his student west; the regents appoint Dewey instructor in philosophy in July. He is twenty-four. In November he joins the First Congregational Church of Ann Arbor, leads Bible classes, and lectures to students on faith, doubt, and Christ. The roll will record him dismissed without letter on the thirtieth of March 1898, by which time he has been in Chicago four years. In the department he begins gathering the men who will follow him there: James Hayden Tufts, George Herbert Mead, James Rowland Angell.
suggested_refs: Membership Roll 1847-1906, First Congregational Church of Ann Arbor Records
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1884.07.19 and 1884.11.02

stops.name: Fenton, the marriage at the Riggs house
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1886.07.28, citing the Ann Arbor Courier of 4 August 1886 and the Fenton Independent of 31 July 1886, and entry 1887.07.19 for the son's birth. A widely repeated claim that this son died in childhood is false and is not carried here: he died in New York in 1967.
stops.campa: In the Fenton house of her grandparents, Mr. and Mrs. F. F. Riggs, he marries Harriet Alice Chipman. The Ann Arbor Courier carries the notice the following week and the Fenton Independent has it too; on the Monday the couple leave for a trip down the St. Lawrence. Alice will teach in his school and run it, and the work of the next twenty years is done by the two of them. They come back to this same house in July of the next year for the birth of their first son, Frederick Archibald. The textbook Psychology appears that year as well.
suggested_refs: The Riggs house at Fenton, Michigan; Dewey's Psychology (1887), Early Works vol. 2
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1886.07.28, 1887, 1887.07.19, and 1967.07.28

stops.name: Minneapolis, the chair of mental and moral philosophy
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1888.02 and 1888-1889, with the daughter's birth at 1889.03.05. Day of the appointment not given, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Called to the chair of Mental and Moral Philosophy and Logic at the University of Minnesota, he moves the household west for what turns out to be a single academic year. The daughter Evelyn Riggs is born in Minneapolis on the fifth of March. In April word comes from Ann Arbor that Morris is dead and that the Michigan chair, his own teacher's chair, is open to him. He accepts inside a fortnight. The household is packed again before the daughter is two months old.
suggested_refs: University of Minnesota faculty records, 1888-1889
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1888.02, 1888-1889, 1889.03.05

stops.name: Ann Arbor, the chair and the grave
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1889.04.19, citing the Proceedings of the Board of Regents, April 1889, 298, and entry 1891.04.10 for the father's death, citing the Washtenaw County death certificate and the University of Michigan Daily of 22 April 1891.
stops.campa: He comes back to Michigan at twenty-nine to hold the chair of the man who taught him Hegel in Baltimore. For five years he runs the department, writes on ethics and on psychology, and takes the train down to Chicago whenever the settlement houses or the schools give him occasion. On the tenth of April 1891 his father dies in Ann Arbor of heart failure. Archibald Sprague Dewey, grocer of Burlington, is buried out of the town where his son teaches philosophy, and the University of Michigan Daily runs the notice on the twenty-second.
suggested_refs: Washtenaw County death certificate of Archibald Sprague Dewey, April 1891
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1889.04.19 and 1891.04.10

stops.name: Plymouth, the summer school of applied ethics
stops.date_confidence: reported rather than documented. William James's atlas file names Dewey on the faculty of Felix Adler's 1891 summer school on the Massachusetts shore, and Adler's file corroborates the roster while flagging the participation of both men as reported. Month defaulted; the pin marks Plymouth, no venue-level site established. The 1938 Adler lecture is a dossier claim, not found in the Adler file.
stops.campa: On the Massachusetts shore Felix Adler runs a summer school of applied ethics, and the roster names both William James and John Dewey. What passed between the two of them there is not on record; that both were on the list is. The Ethical Culture movement Adler founded is doing on Sunday mornings what Dewey has begun to think a school ought to do all week, teaching conduct without a creed. He will give the first annual Adler lecture forty-seven years later. Dewey is thirty-one this summer and known chiefly for a textbook. James is forty-nine.
suggested_refs: Felix Adler's summer school of applied ethics, Plymouth, Massachusetts, 1891
sources: william_james.journey.json
felix_adler.journey.json
john_dewey dossier, uncorroborated for the 1938 lecture

stops.name: Hull House, the ward on Halsted Street
stops.date_confidence: attested, but the tenure is muddled in the secondary literature. The chronology lists him with the Hull-House board of trustees at 1889, records attendance at board meetings on 1897.07.27 and 1897.10.12, and has him resigning from the board on 1903.04.14 for a year on the advisory council. A commonly repeated 1897 election to a Hull-House Association does not appear in the chronology at all; that phrase occurs nowhere in it.
stops.campa: Eight hundred South Halsted Street, a settlement house in a ward of Italian, Greek, Bohemian, and Russian Jewish immigrants, kept by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr. Dewey is carried with its trustees from 1889, lectures there on psychology and on history, and keeps coming back through the whole Chicago decade; the minutes have him at board meetings in July and October of 1897, and in April 1903 he resigns the board for the advisory council. What he learns in that ward he will call democracy for the rest of his life, meaning a way of living near other people rather than a way of voting.
stops.quote: I believe that education is the fundamental method of social progress and reform.
suggested_refs: Hull-House Minutes, Jane Addams Memorial Collection, University of Illinois Chicago
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1889, 1892.01.21, 1897.07.27, 1897.10.12, 1903.04.14
My Pedagogic Creed, full text, English Wikisource

stops.name: University of Chicago, the combined department
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1894.03.19 for the acceptance. No Chicago salary figure appears in the chronology: the often quoted five thousand dollars belongs to the Columbia offer of 1904.05.02 and is not repeated here.
stops.campa: William Rainey Harper, building a university with Rockefeller money on the flat ground south of the city, offers Dewey the head of one department combining philosophy, psychology, and pedagogy. He accepts in March and moves in the autumn. The pedagogy is the whole point: no American university has yet set the study of teaching inside the study of mind and knowledge. Chicago in 1894 is a city of a million and a half with the Pullman strike in its rail yards and the world's fair still standing half dismantled in Jackson Park.
stops.quote: I believe that all education proceeds by the participation of the individual in the social consciousness of the race.
suggested_refs: University of Chicago Register, 1894-95, department of philosophy, psychology and pedagogy
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1894 and 1894.03.19
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, John Dewey
My Pedagogic Creed, full text, English Wikisource

stops.name: Hyde Park, the University Elementary School opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, January 1896; day defaulted to 01. Chronology entry 1896 and Ida B. DePencier, The History of the Laboratory Schools (1967). The 1899 book and the American Psychological Association presidency are attested for that year.
stops.campa: In January the University Elementary School opens with sixteen pupils and Alice Chipman Dewey as its principal. The children cook, weave, and work in wood, and the school subjects reach them through the work: measure and fraction in the recipe, chemistry in the dyeing, history in the loom. Dewey calls these the occupations and holds they are not relief from study but the form study should take. In 1899 he publishes The School and Society, and the same year the American Psychological Association elects him its president.
stops.quote: I believe that the school must represent present life--life as real and vital to the child as that which he carries on in the home, in the neighborhood, or on the playground.
stops.quote_source: My Pedagogic Creed (1897), Article II, quoted whole; the sentence is often printed cut short at the word home
suggested_refs: Ida B. DePencier, The History of the Laboratory Schools: The University of Chicago 1896-1965
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1896 and 1899
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, John Dewey
My Pedagogic Creed, full text, English Wikisource

stops.name: Chicago, the creed and the circuit
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for My Pedagogic Creed and to 1896 for the reflex arc paper, Psychological Review 3 (1896); the chronology dates the latter to July 1896. Days defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He publishes My Pedagogic Creed, a confession of faith laid out as a syllabus, every paragraph opening with the words I believe. The year before, in the Psychological Review, he had taken apart the reflex arc, the picture of a mind as a chain running from stimulus to idea to response, and argued that the chain is a circuit: the seeing already contains the reaching, and the burnt hand changes what the flame looks like. The creed carries that same argument over into a schoolroom. It runs to five articles.
stops.quote: I believe that education, therefore, is a process of living and not a preparation for future living.
suggested_refs: The Reflex Arc Concept in Psychology, Psychological Review 3 (1896)
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1896 and 1897
My Pedagogic Creed, full text, English Wikisource

stops.name: Chicago, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1904.04.05, citing the University of Chicago University Record, May 1904, 35, and Dewey correspondence of 5, 6, and 11 April 1904. The reading of who forced what remains contested and is not settled here.
stops.campa: The Laboratory School is merged with Colonel Francis Parker's school and its staff, Alice is pushed out of the principalship of the combined institution, and on the fifth of April Dewey writes his resignation from the university. The story told afterward is that Harper fired his wife; the papers show an administrative tangle in which nobody is exonerated. Ten years of work end in a letter. His resignation takes effect the first of July and hers the first of October. He is forty-four.
suggested_refs: University of Chicago University Record, May 1904, 35
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1904.04.05

stops.name: Ballinasloe, the son who does not come home
stops.date_confidence: attested that Gordon Chipman Dewey, born Chicago 29 May 1896, was hospitalised at Ballinasloe and died in Ireland on 10 or 11 September 1904, with a memorial service in the Hull-House Theatre on 1 October. The chronology does not state where his father was at the time; the pin marks the hospital town, not a documented location for Dewey himself.
stops.campa: The family sails for Europe in the summer with no post to come back to. In Ireland the second son, Gordon Chipman Dewey, eight years old, born in Chicago the year the school opened, takes typhoid and is put into the hospital at Ballinasloe in County Galway, and there he dies. The record gives two possible days, the tenth and the eleventh of September, and does not say where his father was. On the first of October a memorial service is held for him in the Hull-House Theatre, a continent away, among the people his parents had worked beside.
suggested_refs: Hull-House Theatre memorial service for Gordon Chipman Dewey, 1 October 1904
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1896.05.29, 1904.09.10, 1904.10.01

stops.name: Columbia University, five thousand a year
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1904.05.02 and 1904.05.09, citing the Journal of Philosophy, Psychology and Scientific Methods 1 (12 May 1904): 280. Canonical Columbia pin inherited from henri_bergson.journey.json.
stops.campa: Columbia offers the professorship of philosophy at five thousand dollars, to begin the first of February 1905, and the Journal of Philosophy prints the news within the fortnight. The offer comes on the second of May, four weeks after he wrote his resignation to Harper, and he accepts on the ninth. He is to teach in the philosophy department on Morningside Heights and across the street at Teachers College. He will hold the chair for twenty-six years and the emeritus title for twenty-two more.
suggested_refs: Journal of Philosophy, Psychology and Scientific Methods 1 (12 May 1904): 280
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1904.05.02 and 1904.05.09
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, John Dewey

stops.name: Columbia University, the bibliography for Bergson
stops.date_confidence: attested through the interlock: henri_bergson.journey.json records that Columbia's 1913 welcome gift to Bergson was a bibliography of his writings introduced by Dewey, and Dewey's own dossier states the same and places a meeting in New York that February. Day defaulted to 01. The lecture series grouping James, Russell, and Bergson is a dossier claim, not verified against a syllabus.
stops.campa: Henri Bergson comes to Columbia to lecture, at the height of his fame, and the university's gift to him is a bibliography of his own writings with an introduction by Dewey. Two accounts of experience stand in the same hall on Morningside Heights: the French one that makes duration the real thing, the American one that makes the remaking of a situation the real thing. Dewey has been giving his students James, Russell, and Bergson together in a single series. Of what the two men said to each other in February nothing survives. What does survive is the bibliography, a list of one philosopher's books handed to him by another.
suggested_refs: The 1913 Columbia bibliography of Bergson's writings, with Dewey's introduction
sources: henri_bergson.journey.json
john_dewey dossier

stops.name: New York, Democracy and Education
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; no day in the sources, defaulted to 01. Quotation verified against the Project Gutenberg text of the first edition, ebook 852.
stops.campa: Democracy and Education comes out in his fifty-seventh year and runs the argument the opposite way from the title. It is not that democracy requires schools. It is that education is how any society goes on existing at all, since each generation dies and the next arrives knowing nothing, so that a community lives by transmission and transmits by communication, and communicating is already an education for everyone in the exchange, the teacher included. He writes this in the third year of the war in Europe, and the book will be translated into Arabic, Persian, Japanese, Korean, Dutch, and Albanian.
stops.quote: Education, in its broadest sense, is the means of this social continuity of life.
suggested_refs: Democracy and Education, first edition 1916; Project Gutenberg ebook 852
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1916
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, John Dewey

segments.name: Two Years and Two Months in the East

stops.name: San Francisco, the Shinyo Maru
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1919.01.23, citing Dewey correspondence of 21 and 22 January 1919.
stops.campa: On sabbatical at fifty-nine he takes ship from San Francisco with Alice aboard the Shinyo Maru. He has held the Columbia chair fifteen years and has never taught outside the United States, and he has never crossed the Pacific. The plan is a season of lecturing in Japan and a look at Japanese schools. The letters written on the pier make arrangements for the spring and say nothing about China, which is not on the itinerary at all. They will not see New York again for two years and eight months.
suggested_refs: Letters from China and Japan, ed. Evelyn Dewey (1920)
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1919.01.23

stops.name: Yokohama, the harbour
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1919.02.09, citing Letters from China and Japan and Lewis Feuer, John Dewey's Sojourn in Japan.
stops.campa: The ship comes into Yokohama harbour on the ninth of February and the private sabbatical turns into a public event. The invitation is from Japanese academics who have read him, and the lectures are to be given at the Imperial University of Tokyo. Japan has come out of the war on the winning side and is in the middle of its liberal decade. He admires the schools. The courtesy shown him is unbroken, banquet after banquet, and in the letters home he keeps asking what any of it will come to.
suggested_refs: Lewis S. Feuer, John Dewey's Sojourn in Japan
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1919.02.09

stops.name: Tokyo, the Imperial Hotel
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1919.02.10 and 1919.02.11 for the hotel, the interview, and the move to Nitobe's house; 1919.04.22 and 1919.04.26 for Kyoto; 1919.04.27-28 for Kobe and the Kumano Maru.
stops.campa: They put up at the Imperial Hotel, where Riichiro Hoashi interviews him, and the next day he calls on the president of Tokyo Imperial University. Within the week the household moves into the home of Dr. Inazo Nitobe. In April they go on to Kyoto, where he visits schools and sits as guest of honour at a banquet given by the university president. Former students of his from Columbia have been writing from China. On the twenty-seventh he lectures to teachers at Kobe, and the next day he boards the Kumano Maru.
suggested_refs: Inazo Nitobe's Tokyo house, where the Deweys lodged in February 1919
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1919.02.10, 1919.02.11, 1919.04.22, 1919.04.26, 1919.04.27-28

stops.name: Shanghai, four days before the fourth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1919.04.30, citing Millard's Review 8 (3 May 1919): 365, and entries 1919.05.03-04 for the lecture. The pin marks the old West Gate district: the Kiangsu Educational Association building could not be fixed to a modern address.
stops.campa: He lands at Shanghai on the thirtieth of April. Four days later the students of Peking march against the award of Shantung to Japan, and the May Fourth movement begins while the visitor is still unpacking his trunks. At the Kiangsu Educational Association building by the old West Gate he lectures on the relation between democracy and education. Student stenographers take the lecture down; it is translated, printed in the newspapers, and read in provinces he will never reach. He had booked passage home for the summer.
stops.quote: education is not an affair of 'telling' and being told, but an active and constructive process
stops.quote_source: Democracy and Education (1916), Chapter Three; lowercase opening as it stands mid-sentence in the source
suggested_refs: The Kiangsu Educational Association building, Laoximen, Shanghai
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1919.04.30 and 1919.05.03-04
Democracy and Education, Project Gutenberg ebook 852

stops.name: Hangzhou, dinner with Sun Yat-sen
stops.date_confidence: the dinner is attested at chronology entry 1919.05.09, citing Zhenhuan Zou, The Dewey Fever, 46, but the entry gives no location. Hangchow is an inference from the surrounding 1919.05.05-09 window; against it, the chronology puts him in Shanghai on 11 May, records a second dinner with Sun Yat-sen on 12 May, and Sun was resident in Shanghai through 1919. The pin is therefore contested and should be read as the Hangchow window, not a documented address.
stops.campa: He is in Hangchow for five days in the second week of May, lecturing under the provincial educational association, and on the ninth he dines with Hu Shih, who studied under him at Columbia and now leads the movement for a written language people actually speak, with Jiang Menglin, another of his students, and with Sun Yat-sen. The republic is six years old and coming apart, and the question at the table is whether it can be rebuilt from the schools upward instead of from the presidential palace down. The entry gives the date and the four names and no address; two days later he is in Shanghai.
suggested_refs: Zhenhuan Zou, The Dewey Fever, 46
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1919.05.05-09, 1919.05.09, 1919.05.11, 1919.05.12

stops.name: Peking, 135 Morrison Street
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1919.05.30, 1919.09.04, 1921.06 for the residence and the farewell address, 1919.07.28 for the Tientsin conference, 1919.11.02 and 1919.11.09 for the week in Mukden, and 1919.05.14 and 1920.04.04-06 for the Nanking lectures.
stops.campa: He comes up to Peking at the end of May and stays the better part of two years, first in the Edwards house inside the YMCA compound, afterward in a flat at 135 Morrison Street. He lectures at the National University and the Teachers College dozens of times on ethics, education, and the logic of inquiry, with Hu Shih beside him turning each sentence into Chinese. In July he sits at Tientsin with the heads of the higher schools over how to reopen what the strike has closed. He goes north to Mukden for a week, and south to Nanking for a series on the Sophists and Plato that runs to nineteen lectures.
stops.quote: Not only does social life demand teaching and learning for its own permanence, but the very process of living together educates.

stops.name: New York, home after two years and two months
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1921.09.28, citing Dewey correspondence of 12 October 1921. The Chinese honorifics are attested; the Maoist denunciation after 1949 and the post-Mao revival are carried from the dossier and a general encyclopaedia account and were not independently traced to a specific campaign document.
stops.campa: He comes home in September, two years and two months after the Shanghai landing, by way of Canton and the Pacific. He is sixty-two. Behind him are some two hundred lectures taken down by student stenographers and printed across the provinces, and a generation of Chinese teachers who called him Mr. Democracy, Mr. Science, and the American Confucius. Within thirty years the schools of the People's Republic will teach that Deweyism is the ideology of American imperialism, and those same lecture notes will serve as evidence for the prosecution.

stops.name: Constantinople, the survey of a one-year-old republic
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1924.06 and 1924.08.01-02 for Constantinople and Bursa, 1924.07 and 1924.08.22 for Angora and the teachers' congress. Days defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The Turkish republic, one year old, asks him to look at its schools and say what a national system ought to be. He arrives in Constantinople in the summer, crosses to Bursa, spends about two weeks in Angora where the government now sits and joins the congress of the Union of Teachers, and comes back to the old capital to dine with the head of Near East Relief and lunch at the Palace Hotel. The report he files asks for teacher training, for libraries, and for one unified public school system paid for out of the state.

stops.name: Mexico City, the summer school and the heart attack
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1926.07.05-08.21 for the summer school, 1926.08 for Cuernavaca and Alice's heart attack, 1926.08.23 for Lake Chapala. The pin marks the old downtown campus of the National University.
stops.campa: From the fifth of July to the twenty-first of August he teaches two courses at the summer school of the National University, meets the education minister Jose Manuel Puig Casauranc, and writes for American readers about the church and state war the Calles government is fighting while he lectures. In August the household goes out to Cuernavaca, where Alice has a heart attack. On the twenty-third they move on to Lake Chapala, and then back to the Hotel Geneve in the capital. She is nearly seventy and does not get her strength back.
suggested_refs: Dewey's 1926 articles on church and state in Mexico, Later Works vol. 2

stops.name: New York, the death of Alice Chipman Dewey
stops.date_confidence: contested. The chronology gives 14 July 1927 and arteriosclerosis, citing Notable American Women, 466, and Dewey correspondence of that day; other reference works give 13 July and a cerebral thrombosis. Neither the day nor the cause is settled here. The chronology gives only New York, with no address, so the pin is the city.
stops.campa: Alice Chipman Dewey dies in New York. The chronology gives the fourteenth of July and arteriosclerosis; other reference works give the thirteenth and a cerebral thrombosis, and the difference in the day and in the cause has not been resolved. Forty-one years of marriage, a school built together and lost together, a son buried in Ireland. He is sixty-seven. He does not write about it in anything published. Nine days later he goes north to Nova Scotia.
suggested_refs: Notable American Women, entry on Alice Chipman Dewey, 466
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1927.07.14

stops.name: Hubbards, the summers on the Nova Scotia shore
stops.date_confidence: attested as a recurring pattern; chronology entries 1927.07.23, 1929.09, 1930.06.10-07.21, 1937.07.15-09.14, 1938.07.28, 1946.07.10, 1948.07.15 among many. The 1946 fall is attested verbatim at 1946.09.21 but the chronology does not locate it; the next entry has him back in New York after returning from Cape Breton, several hundred kilometres from this pin.
stops.campa: Nine days after her death he goes up to Hubbards on the Nova Scotia shore, and for the next twenty years the summers are spent there, first with his children and later with Roberta: the wooden house, the cold water, the boats. July after July the chronology fills with it, on through 1948. The missions and commissions of the public life are run out of this house half the year. At eighty-six he is still climbing about on Cape Breton rock, and in September 1946 he slips there and dislocates his left shoulder, and writes about it two days later in a tone of mild interest.
suggested_refs: The Dewey summer house at Hubbards, Nova Scotia
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1927.07.23, 1946.09.21, 1946.09.30, 1948.07.15

stops.name: Moscow, the schools of the new state
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1928.06.28 to 1928.07.09 for Berlin and Leningrad and the Hermitage, 1928.07.13, 1928.07.18, 1928.07.21 for Moscow. His later renunciation of Soviet policy is documented in his own writings and in the 1937 commission work; it is not stated in these entries.
stops.campa: He goes into the Soviet Union with a delegation of American educators, flying by way of Berlin to Leningrad. In Moscow he sits at a conference in the Second University and is received by the Society for Cultural Relations with Foreign Countries. The schools astonish him: children running their own collectives, experiment everywhere, the old classroom gone. The essays he publishes on returning praise the energy and mark the coercion under it, and both halves are held against him afterward. In Leningrad, before any of that, he had spent a week and walked the Hermitage with his daughter Evelyn.
suggested_refs: Impressions of Soviet Russia and the Revolutionary World (1929), Later Works vol. 3
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1928.06.28-1928.07.09, 1928.07.13, 1928.07.18, 1928.07.21

stops.name: Edinburgh, the Roxburghe Hotel and the Gifford Lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1929.04.15, 1929.04.17-05.17, 1929.05.15 for the lodging, the lectures, and the excursion. The retirement in 1930 is attested to the year only.
stops.campa: For five weeks he lodges at the Roxburghe Hotel on Charlotte Square and gives the Gifford Lectures at the university, printed the same year as The Quest for Certainty. The case he puts is that philosophy has spent two thousand years hunting for something exempt from risk, a fixed order to be contemplated rather than a world to be acted in, and that the hunt is a flight from the very sciences it claims to honour. Columbia will retire him the next year, at seventy, with eleven more books still to come. On a free day in May he drives out to see the ruined castle where Mary Queen of Scots was born.
stops.quote: Every great advance in science has issued from a new audacity of imagination.
stops.quote_source: attributed to The Quest for Certainty (1929), chapter XI; carried from the standard citation and not verified against the primary text
suggested_refs: The Quest for Certainty: A Study of the Relation of Knowledge and Action (1929)
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entries 1929.04.15, 1929.04.17-05.17, 1929.05.15, 1930

stops.name: New York, Art as Experience and A Common Faith
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for both books; no day in the sources, defaulted to 01. The Barnes friendship from a 1917 Columbia seminar and the Foundation's self-description as a school rather than a museum are attested; the Foundation's 2012 move to Philadelphia postdates Dewey and is kept out of the stop, see the report.
stops.campa: Two books in one year from a man four years retired. Art as Experience comes out of the rooms at Merion where Albert Barnes, who met him at a Columbia seminar in 1917 and stayed close for three decades, hangs Cezannes for students instead of visitors and insists the place is a school and not a museum. The argument is that a work of art is not an object but something that happens between a person and an object, on the same continuum as any experience carried through to its end. A Common Faith, published the same year by a man off the church rolls since 1898, says the religious quality of experience can be had without the supernatural.
suggested_refs: The Barnes Foundation collection at Merion, Pennsylvania, as Dewey knew it
sources: Barbara Levine, comp., Chronology of John Dewey's Life and Work, Center for Dewey Studies, Southern Illinois University Carbondale, updated 2016, entry 1934

stops.name: Cape Town, Table Mountain and the Fellowship
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1934.05.26 for the sailing from Gibraltar aboard the Rex, 1934.06.14 for the arrival and Table Mountain, 1934.06.16-21 for Durban, 1934.07.01 for the return by train, 1934.07.02-13 for the conference. Latitude here is negative: a dossier coordinate with the sign dropped plotted this stop in northern Iraq.
stops.campa: He crosses from Gibraltar aboard the Rex, lands at Capetown, and goes up Table Mountain the day he arrives. He is seventy-four. The occasion is the international conference of the New Education Fellowship, and in July he addresses it on the need for a philosophy of education. In between he takes ship and rail for Durban and comes back across the country by train. The conference meets in a state whose schooling is organised by race, and among the South Africans on its programme are Jan Hofmeyr, Jan Smuts, and Hendrik Verwoerd.

stops.name: Johannesburg, the honorary degree and the flight north
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1934.07.15-27, 1934.07.24 for the degree, which the chronology credits to Johannesburg University rather than by the Witwatersrand name, 1934.07.28 and 1934.07.31 for Victoria Falls and Zimbabwe, 1934.08.02, 1934.08.03, 1934.08.04, 1934.08.06. Latitudes for both this stop and the Falls are negative; the dossier had dropped both signs. That he published little afterward on segregated schooling is an absence noted by later scholarship, not a chronology entry.
stops.campa: Three weeks are worked out of Johannesburg: the Fellowship again, an address to the Farmer Labor Federation, an honorary degree on the twenty-fourth, a talk to the Philosophical Society of the University of the Witwatersrand. What he published afterward about the country's segregated schooling comes to very little. On the twenty-eighth he flies north to Victoria Falls at seventy-four, goes up the river in a launch, and flies on to the Zimbabwe ruins and Buluwayo before turning back. He addresses Pretoria on the fourth of August and leaves Johannesburg on the sixth.

segments.name: Coyoacan and the Fifth Avenue Apartment

stops.name: Coyoacan, the first session in the blue house
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entries 1937.03.19 for the agreement to serve and 1937.04.10-17 for the hearings, which the chronology locates only as Mexico City. The published transcript gives the venue as Avenida Londres 127, Coyoacan. Canonical Casa Azul pin inherited from leon_trotsky.journey.json. The house was the Kahlo family's, lent to Trotsky and Natalia Sedova from January 1937; the frequent description of it as Rivera's home is wrong for these years, since Rivera moved in only in 1941.
stops.campa: Seventy-seven years old, he agrees on the nineteenth of March to head the Commission of Inquiry into the Charges Made against Leon Trotsky, and by the tenth of April he is sitting as its chairman in the dining room of the blue house on Avenida Londres, the Kahlo family house lent since January to Trotsky and Natalia Sedova. The windows are barricaded. Moscow has condemned the man in his absence and shot the others. The commission can compel nobody and enforce nothing; it can only take testimony in public, and the chairman opens by saying what that is for.
stops.quote: The right to a hearing before condemnation is such an elementary right in every civilized country that it would be absurd for us to reassert it were it not for the efforts which have been made to prevent Mr. Trotsky from being heard, and the efforts that now are being made to discredit the work of this Commission of Inquiry.
stops.quote_source: Dewey as chairman, First Session, Coyoacan, 10 April 1937, transcript at marxists.org
suggested_refs: The Case of Leon Trotsky: Report of Hearings on the Charges Made against Him in the Moscow Trials (1937)

stops.name: Coyoacan, the thirteenth session
stops.date_confidence: attested; the transcript records thirteen sessions held 10 to 17 April 1937. On Carleton Beals: he put his question at the afternoon session of 16 April and sent his resignation the next morning, and the transcript files it under the twelfth session, so the common phrase that he resigned after the eleventh is loose. The December 1937 finding of not guilty is carried from the dossier and the commission's published report, not from the chronology entry.
stops.campa: Thirteen sessions in eight days: terrorism, sabotage, the Comintern, dates and passports and border crossings, Trotsky answering in his own English, Dewey holding the room to the rules of evidence. On the sixteenth Carleton Beals, one of the commissioners, puts a question suggesting Trotsky had sent an agent into Mexico in 1919, and the following morning he resigns and goes to the newspapers calling the inquiry a whitewash. The commission finishes without him. In December, in New York, it reports that the Moscow trials were frame-ups and that the accused man is not guilty.
stops.quote: Our sole function is to ascertain the truth as far as is humanly possible.
stops.quote_source: Dewey as chairman, opening statement, First Session, Coyoacan, 10 April 1937, transcript at marxists.org

stops.name: New York, Experience and Education
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for both books; day defaulted to 01. The first annual Felix Adler lecture in 1938 is a dossier claim; it was not found in felix_adler.journey.json or in the chronology excerpt consulted, and is flagged rather than dropped.
stops.campa: Experience and Education and Logic: The Theory of Inquiry come out in the same year, the one a short correction addressed to his own followers, the other a full technical system written at seventy-nine. The small book says plainly that not every experience educates, that some experiences deaden the capacity for having any more of them, and that a teacher who organises nothing has walked off the job. The progressive schools quoting him have been reading him as a permission slip. He gives the first annual Felix Adler lecture the same year, five years after Adler's death.

stops.name: 1158 Fifth Avenue, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1946.12.11, citing the New York Times of 11 and 12 December 1946: the apartment, the hour, the officiant, and Roberta's 1904 birth at Oil City. The pin is the geocode of 1158 Fifth Avenue at East 97th Street, correcting a dossier coordinate 1.6 km south at East 86th.
stops.campa: At ten in the morning, in his apartment at 1158 Fifth Avenue, eighty-seven years old, he marries Estelle Roberta Lowitz Grant, forty-two, born in 1904 at Oil City in Pennsylvania, the town where he taught school for two years before her parents were grown. Jerome Nathanson of the Ethical Culture Society officiates. The Times carries it two days running. The apartment looks over the park at Ninety-Seventh Street, and he will live in it another five and a half years.

stops.name: 1158 Fifth Avenue, the last morning
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1952.06.01, citing Dewey correspondence of that date, control no. 09541. The chronology gives the cause and the day but not the address; that he died at home in New York is stated by the standard reference accounts.
stops.campa: He dies of pneumonia on the first of June, ninety-two years old and four months short of ninety-three, at home in the Fifth Avenue apartment where the second marriage was held. He had written on schools, logic, art, religion, Soviet Russia, Turkish and Mexican schools, the charges against Trotsky, and the theory of inquiry, and had outlived nearly everyone he argued with. The last book came out in 1949. The entry for the day carries a cause of death and the control number of a letter, 09541.
suggested_refs: Dewey correspondence, 1 June 1952, control no. 09541

stops.name: Middle Village, the Fresh Pond Crematory
stops.date_confidence: attested; chronology entry 1952.06.02. The pin is the geocode of 61-40 Mount Olivet Crescent, correcting a dossier coordinate roughly 2 km east. Where the ashes were kept between 1952 and 1972 is not stated by any source reached here.
stops.campa: The body goes out to the Fresh Pond Crematory at Middle Village in Queens, on Mount Olivet Crescent, and is burned the day after the death. No grave is dug and no stone is cut. The chronology records the place and the date and then says nothing further about the ashes for twenty years. Where they were kept in that interval is not stated by the chronology, nor by the biographies, nor by the centre that holds his papers. The next documented fact about them carries the date of the twenty-sixth of October 1972.

stops.name: Ira Allen Chapel, the ashes come back to Burlington
stops.date_confidence: attested, and this corrects a dossier tag that treated the interment as unconfirmed tradition. Chronology entry 1972.10.26 records the programme commemorating the interment of the ashes of John and Roberta Dewey at the University of Vermont, citing Dykhuizen, 322. The 1939 Founder's Day address in this chapel is chronology entry 1939.05.01; the stamp's first-day ceremonies at Burlington are entry 1968.10.21.
stops.campa: An urn is set into a memorial on the north side of the Ira Allen Chapel, on the campus he entered at fifteen, in the town where he was born and given a dead brother's name. The university says it is the only grave site on its grounds. Roberta's ashes are placed there with his. He had come back to this chapel in 1939 to give the Founder's Day address, called Education: 1800-1939, and four years before this interment the post office held the first-day ceremonies for his thirty-cent stamp in Burlington.
stops.quote: Democracy has to be born anew every generation, and education is its midwife.
stops.quote_source: attributed to The Need of an Industrial Education in an Industrial Democracy (1916), Middle Works vol. 10; carried from the standard citation and not verified against the primary text
